notes.h: What it is and how it is weighted
notes.b: Leaving Certificate Biology is not assessed by a single exam. Alongside the written paper there is a second component in which you do your own scientific investigation, so it is worth knowing how the two fit together.
points: Leaving Certificate Biology has two assessment components: a written examination worth 60%, taken at Higher and Ordinary level, and an additional assessment component, the Biology in Practice Investigation, worth 40%.

The investigation is based on one common brief (the same task for all students) and is worth 200 marks. It is assessed at the level at which you take the written paper, so only the written examination has two levels.
Both components are set and examined by the State Examinations Commission (SEC), the body that runs the state exams. The investigation is not coursework marked by your own teacher.

You complete the work during the course and, in Year 2 (sixth year), submit to the SEC evidence of your ability to conduct scientific research on a particular issue and to use appropriate primary data (data you collect yourself) to investigate aspects of that issue.
The specification envisages that the investigation will take up to 20 hours to complete. Further details are given in the Guidelines for the Biology in Practice Investigation.
notes.tip: Don't say the investigation is set at Higher and Ordinary level or marked by your teacher: it has a common brief and is submitted to and examined by the SEC.

notes.b: The investigation is there to let you show what you have learned across the whole course, not to test one topic. It also builds the habits of a working scientist.
points: It gives you an opportunity to display evidence of your learning throughout the course, in particular the learning in the Unifying Strand (Nature of Science): the outcomes in this chapter and in Scientific Knowledge, Science in Society and Biological Reasoning.

It is designed to be integrated into the flow of teaching and learning, to be motivating and relevant, and to show the relevance of biology to students’ lives, so it uses real issues rather than abstract ones.
It also draws together the learning outcomes and the cross-cutting themes of Health, Sustainability and Technology, which run through every strand of the course.

It lets you pursue your own interests in biology, make your own investigative decisions, gain a depth of conceptual understanding and self-regulate your learning (plan, monitor and adjust it yourself).

The specification stresses that research and experimentation are “more about engaging with and learning from the process, rather than seeking a perfect answer”. This is why an experiment that does not go to plan can still be valuable.

You should give an authentic account of how your investigative work unfolded, discuss and explain the outcomes, and say how you might revise aspects of the process. There is more on this in Reflecting on investigations.
notes.tip: Because the aim is learning from the process, an honest account of what went wrong and what you would change is worth more than pretending the experiment was perfect.

notes.b: Every year the SEC publishes a brief, the document that tells you exactly what the investigation must cover. It is the starting point for everything you do.
points: The SEC publishes an Investigation Brief every year, in term two of Year 1 (fifth year) of the course, so you have time to plan; the brief for the 2027 examination was issued in January 2026.
The 2027 brief is set on membranes, osmosis and food preservation.
The brief sets out the specific requirements of the investigation for that year, so it is the final word on what you must do.
It allows you to develop your thinking and ideas on areas related to the brief that you would like to pursue.
It helps teachers and students plan, and includes stimulus material (articles, data or images) to set a context for the investigation.

It allows you to develop an investigative log (a running record of your work and decisions) that you can draw on as you complete the investigation. There is more on this in Reflecting on investigations.
notes.tip: Any detail about word counts, deadlines or formats comes from the SEC brief and Guidelines for that year, so check them rather than relying on memory.

notes.h: The two parts of the work
notes.b: The work has two parts, followed by an evidence-based argument and a submitted report. Using both research and an experiment is what makes it more than just a lab write-up.
points: Part 1 is scientific research on an issue related to the brief, so you start by reading, not experimenting. You gather, process and evaluate information from secondary sources (work done by others, such as articles and reports), and what you learn may help to inform your experimental work.
Evaluating how reliable those sources are, including checking for bias, matters because a weak source weakens your whole argument. There is more on this in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.

Part 2 is an experiment related to an issue within the brief, which gives you primary data of your own. You generate a hypothesis (a testable prediction), plan and design the experiment, carry it out and gather primary data, then analyse the data and form conclusions.
The skills for Part 2 are in Questioning and predicting, Designing and conducting investigations, Objectivity and data quality and Producing and analysing data.

You then develop an evidence-based argument in response to the brief, drawing on both your research and your experiment, so each part supports your case, because research gives the background and the experiment gives your own evidence.

On completion you submit a report of the investigation in Year 2, in a format prescribed by the SEC. General report-writing skills are in Communicating results, but the SEC sets the actual format, so follow its instructions rather than your own layout.

Schools have a high degree of autonomy in planning and organising the completion of the investigation. A separate document, Guidelines for the Biology in Practice Investigation, gives guidance on its organisation, implementation and oversight.
notes.tip: Don't describe the investigation as only an experiment: it has research from secondary sources, an experiment with primary data, and an evidence-based argument.

notes.b: The specification sums up what the investigation asks of you in four requirements. They are also the reasons the descriptors of quality look the way they do.
points: It requires you to consider issues related to real-world applications of biology, such as how biological ideas are used in health, sustainability or technology.
It requires you to demonstrate investigative skills, such as the planning, practical and analysis skills used to answer a scientific question.
It requires you to relate your investigative work to the work of scientists in society, for example by asking how professionals would tackle the same question.
It requires you to communicate your findings appropriately and effectively.

notes.h: The 2027 report: how the 200 marks are allocated
notes.b: The SEC brief sets the report's headings, limits and format, and allocates the 200 marks in four blocks of 50. The descriptors of quality that follow describe the standard expected within them.
points: Criterion A, 50 marks: title and introduction, research question and hypothesis, background research and evaluation of secondary data, and references.
Criterion B, 50 marks: designing and planning, and conducting the experiment, including safety, fairness, accuracy and choice of equipment.
Criterion C, 50 marks: primary data and its presentation, data analysis, and conclusions.

Criterion D, 50 marks: scientific literacy, so it rewards good writing and thinking throughout (communication, coherence, relevance and a reflective approach), which is judged across the whole report rather than in one section.
notes.tip: Criterion D is not a separate section you can write at the end. Clear, coherent, relevant and reflective writing has to run through the whole report.

notes.h: The 2027 report: format and submission rules
notes.b: Besides the marks, the 2027 brief fixes exactly how the report must look and how it is handed in. Following these rules is part of doing the task properly.
points: The report uses seven numbered headings, each on a new page: Title and Introduction; Background Research; Designing and Planning; Conducting the Experiment; Data and Data Analysis; Conclusions; References.
The report body is no more than 1,500 words, so you must be concise (references, data tables, formulae, equations and labels are not counted), with no more than 20 images and no video.
Text is Arial and black, with 14-point bold headings and 12-point body text at 1.5 line spacing, portrait pages, 20 mm margins with nothing in them, and page numbers at the bottom centre.
The experiment and primary data collection are carried out under the direct supervision of the biology teacher, and every source, including any use of AI, is referenced.

The completed SEC cover page goes first. The report is converted to PDF, printed and proof-read, then given to the teacher by Friday 26 February 2027 with Authentication Form P.2 signed by the student, teacher and principal.

notes.b: The SEC judges the quality of your work against four descriptors, each with a high, moderate and low level. The first is about how well you understand the biology behind your investigation.
points: High: you engage thoroughly with the concepts being investigated; explain clearly and accurately, using appropriate means, the biological phenomena involved; and, where applicable, pose a testable hypothesis that is underpinned by biological theory and clearly describe the purpose of the investigation.
Moderate: you show good engagement with the concepts; describe the biological phenomena involved; and, where applicable, pose a testable hypothesis and outline the purpose of the investigation.
Low: you show limited engagement with the concepts; outline the biological phenomena involved; and are provided with a testable hypothesis to investigate rather than making your own.
notes.tip: To reach the high level, explain the biology clearly and accurately instead of just describing it, and base your hypothesis on biological theory.

notes.h: Descriptor 2: investigative skills, design and method
notes.b: The second descriptor is about how well you planned and carried out the experiment, because good data can only come from a good design.
points: High: you use clear, thorough and appropriate investigative design and methods to collect primary data, leading to high quality data, presentation and analysis, because good data can only come from a good method.
Moderate: you use clear and appropriate design and methods, leading to good quality data, presentation and analysis.
Low: your design and methods are unclear, leading to limited data, presentation and analysis.

notes.h: Descriptor 3: investigative skills, analysis and conclusions
notes.b: The third descriptor is about what you do with your results: whether your conclusions follow from the data and whether you recognise the weaknesses in your own design.
points: High: you draw valid conclusions that are justified by the data and relate to any hypotheses made, and thoroughly evaluate the investigation, acknowledging sources of error in the investigative design, so your evaluation must be honest and specific.
Moderate: you draw conclusions that relate to any hypotheses made, and identify potential sources of error in the investigative design.
Low: you draw limited conclusions, and potential sources of error in the investigative design are not identified.
notes.tip: Link every conclusion back to your hypothesis and to your data, and name the sources of error in your design instead of leaving them out.

notes.h: Descriptor 4: relating investigative work to the work of scientists in society
notes.b: The fourth descriptor looks beyond your own experiment. It asks how your findings connect to what scientists do and to wider issues in society.
points: High: you offer a considered reflection that locates the outcomes of the investigation within broader issues relating to the work of a scientist or science and society.
Moderate: you reflect on how the outcomes relate to the work of a scientist or science and society.
Low: you make limited links between the outcomes and the work of a scientist or science and society, so your findings stay isolated from the wider picture.

notes.b: This is study advice drawn from the wording of the descriptors, not an SEC rule. Reading the four descriptors side by side shows what moves work from one level to the next.
points: The differences between levels are in the verbs and qualifiers: “explain clearly and accurately” against “describe” against “outline”; “thoroughly evaluate” against “identify” against not identifying errors; and “considered reflection” within “broader issues” against “limited links”.
Posing your own testable hypothesis, grounded in biological theory, is a feature of the high and moderate levels. Being given a hypothesis is described at the low level.

Acknowledging and evaluating sources of error in the design is expected for high achievement. A perfect result is not required, but an honest evaluation is, because it shows you understand how reliable your results are. This fits the specification’s stress on learning from the process.

The fourth descriptor needs explicit links between your own findings and the work of scientists or wider issues in science and society, for example how scientists would investigate the same issue on a larger scale, or the health, sustainability or technology issue in the brief.
notes.tip: Aim your wording at the high-level verbs: explain, thoroughly evaluate and give a considered reflection, rather than just describe, identify or outline.

keyTerms.definition: The additional assessment component, worth 40%, in which students research an issue, carry out an experiment and submit a report to the SEC.
The document published by the SEC every year, setting out the specific requirements of that year’s investigation.
The NCCA's four criteria, with high, moderate and low wording, that describe the quality expected in the Biology in Practice Investigation.
A response to the brief that draws on both the student’s research and experiment to support its conclusions.
Material included in the Investigation Brief to set the context for the investigation.

questions.prompt: Outline the two parts of the work students carry out for the Biology in Practice Investigation.
questions.model: The first part is scientific research on an issue related to the brief, in which students gather, process and evaluate information from secondary sources. The second part is an experiment related to an issue within the brief, in which students generate a hypothesis, plan and design the experiment, carry it out and gather primary data, then analyse the data and form conclusions. Students then develop an evidence-based argument in response to the brief, drawing on both their research and their experiment, and submit a report to the SEC in Year 2.

questions.prompt: Describe three features of the Investigation Brief published by the SEC.
questions.model: First, the SEC publishes the brief every year, in term two of Year 1 of the course. Second, the brief sets out the specific requirements of the investigation for that year. Third, the brief includes stimulus material to set a context for the investigation. The brief also helps teachers and students plan, lets students pursue their own ideas on related areas, and allows students to develop an investigative log that they can draw on as they complete the investigation.

questions.prompt: Using the descriptors of quality, explain what distinguishes high from moderate achievement in investigative skills (analysis and conclusions) and in relating investigative work to the work of scientists in society.
questions.model: For investigative skills in analysis and conclusions, high achievement draws valid conclusions that are justified by the data and relate to any hypotheses made, and thoroughly evaluates the investigation, acknowledging sources of error in the design. Moderate achievement draws conclusions that relate to any hypotheses made and identifies potential sources of error in the design. The difference lies in the qualifiers: valid and justified conclusions, and a thorough evaluation, at high level, against conclusions that merely relate to the hypothesis and an identification of errors at moderate level. For relating the work to scientists in society, high achievement offers a considered reflection that locates the outcomes within broader issues relating to the work of a scientist or science and society. Moderate achievement reflects on how the outcomes relate to that work. The high level goes further, with a considered reflection placed within broader issues, for example by showing how scientists would investigate the same issue on a larger scale.
